## Goals

. . .

:::{.nonincremental}
- A GPU is **not a faster CPU**: the opposite bet.
- `CuArray` ≠ `Array`: the **bus** can cost more than the maths.
- **Feed the GPU**: when it pays off, when it *loses*.
- **Coalescing**: locality on the card.
:::

. . .

# Part A — moving to the card {style="text-align: center;"}

## Two strategies for the same problem

. . .

Same wall: **memory is far away**. Opposite bets.

. . .

| | **CPU** | **GPU** |
|---|---|---|
| threads | **few**, fast | **thousands**, slow |
| caches | **big** (24 MiB L3) | **small** |
| hides the wait by | **caching** | **switching** threads |

. . .

> CPU **avoids** the wait, GPU **covers** it. Too little work: [the wait shows.]{style="background-color: yellow;"}

::: {.notes}
GPU: when one group of threads waits on memory, another group runs. With too little
work there is nobody to switch to.
:::

## Same code, different hardware

. . .

```julia
Ag = cu(A)          # copy to VRAM
Bg = cu(B)

A  * B              # CPU
Ag * Bg             # GPU: the SAME `*`
```

- **Multiple dispatch** picks the GPU method.
- [**The algorithm didn't change.**]{style="background-color: yellow;"}

::: {.notes}
VRAM = the card's own memory; the bus links RAM and VRAM. `*` is a generic function;
its arguments are now CuArrays. That is the dispatch module's promise, cashed in.
:::

## The array changed, even if the code didn't

. . .

```julia
A  = rand(3, 3)     # Matrix{Float64}, RAM
Ag = cu(A)          # CuArray{Float32,…}, VRAM
```

- `cu` **copies** across the bus: two objects, two memories.
- Float64 → **Float32** (`CuArray(A)` keeps Float64).
- `Ag[1]` is an **error**: one element = one bus round trip.

. . .

> ▶ Script: cell "4. The GPU — a CuArray is NOT a CPU array"

. . .

> The type change is [a **copy you paid for**]{style="background-color: yellow;"}.

::: {.notes}
Dispatch picked the GPU method because the type changed. Measured live: typeof(Ag)
prints CuArray{Float32, 2, CUDACore.DeviceMemory}. Float32 is the card's native
precision; the Float64 -> Float32 narrowing is the most common "why are my results
different on GPU" question. Scalar indexing throws by design (CUDA.@allowscalar
overrides it — mention only if asked).
:::

## What the copy costs {.smaller}

. . .

Two 4096² Float32 matrices (64 MiB each):

. . .

| step | time |
|---|---|
| host → device, `cu(A)` | 8.5 ms |
| compute, `Ag * Bg` | **35 ms** |
| device → host, `Array(Ag)` | [**52 ms**]{style="background-color: yellow;"} |

- Round trip = **1.7× the computation**. **Back** is the expensive way.
- **Don't ping-pong**: upload once, bring back a **scalar**.

. . .

> ▶ Script: cell "What the copy costs"

::: {.notes}
A pipeline that copies back after every step lives on the bus, not on the GPU.
The torch twin (python/4) measures the same shape: ~10 ms up, ~50 ms down,
~28 ms of compute.
:::

# Part B — feed the GPU {style="text-align: center;"}

## The big matmul {.smaller}

. . .

Same `*`, 4096², Float32:

. . .

| | time |
|---|---|
| CPU, `A * B` | hundreds of ms (varies) |
| GPU, `CUDA.@sync Ag * Bg` | **~35 ms**: [**~15–20×**]{style="background-color: yellow;"} |

- `CUDA.@sync`: GPU calls return **immediately** — else you time the launch.
- 1 **FLOP** = one float operation; this matmul = 2·4096³ ≈ 137 G.

. . .

> ▶ Script: cell "The matrix product, CPU vs GPU"

. . .

> Big, regular job: what the GPU wants. **Smaller ones?**

::: {.notes}
The CPU side swings a lot on this laptop (366–942 ms seen in one session, power
profile and hybrid cores); the GPU side is stable at ~35 ms. Quote the order of
magnitude, not one ratio.
:::

## Bet before you look 🎲 {style="text-align: center;"}

. . .

**N × N** matmul, CPU vs GPU, N from **64** to **4096**.

. . .

> ### Does the GPU always win?

. . .

> ▶ Script: cell "5. Feed the GPU — when does it start paying off?"

## When does the GPU start paying off? {.smaller}

. . .

Float32, CPU measured **first**:

. . .

| N | CPU | GPU | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| 64 | 0.01 ms | 0.03 ms | [**0.25×**]{style="background-color: yellow;"} loses |
| 128 | 0.03 ms | 0.03 ms | 1.2× |
| 512 | 1.15 ms | 0.09 ms | 13.0× |
| 2048 | 69.8 ms | 3.02 ms | **23.1×** |
| 4096 | hundreds of ms | ~35 ms | ~15–20× |

- **Q1.** Why slower for small N? Which costs don't depend on N?
- **Q2.** Speedup: grows or plateaus? What's the ceiling?

. . .

> Not **faster**: **wider**.

::: {.notes}
Narrow work doesn't get faster on a wider machine.
Q1 of the script: fixed costs (launch, sync) don't depend on N; at N = 64 the GPU
spends its time being launched. Q2: the speedup peaks (1024–2048), then levels
off — both sides hit their throughput ceiling (the card goes from ~18 to ~5000+
GFLOP/s once the work fills it). The dip at 4096 is not explained here;
plausibly a laptop power/thermal limit. Shape is robust, exact ratios are not.
On a laptop, measure the CPU BEFORE the GPU: they share a power budget, and the
CPU slows down after the GPU has worked (measured once: 75 ms vs 2.97 ms for the
same gemm, throttled).
:::

## Feeding it: the batch, measured {.smaller}

. . .

One layer `W` (4096²) × `B` examples, as in the batching deck:

. . .

| B | GPU **total** | GFLOP/s |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **0.41 ms** | 82.8 |
| 8 | **0.42 ms** | 638 |
| 64 | **0.45 ms** | 4761 |
| 256 | 2.23 ms | 3853 |

- [**B = 1 → 64: 64× the work, < 2× the time.**]{style="background-color: yellow;"}
- At B = 1 the card was **idle**.

. . .

> ▶ Script: cell "Batching on the GPU"

::: {.notes}
Same GPU; we just asked more of it.
Do NOT say "the GPU loses at B=1": measured, it still beats the CPU at B=1.
The honest line is "you are using ~2% of what you paid for" (82.8 vs 4761
GFLOP/s, relative to the best of this run, not the spec sheet). "It loses"
invites "so use a CPU"; "~2%" invites "so batch". B=64 total is run-dependent
(0.45–0.63 ms seen). Torch twin: 0.40 → 0.46 ms, B=1 → 64.
:::

# Part C — coalescing: locality on the card {style="text-align: center;"}

## What a warp wants

. . .

**Warp** = 32 threads in lockstep, loading **together**.

- Neighboring addresses → **few** transactions. [Coalesced.]{style="background-color: yellow;"}
- Scattered addresses → **one per thread**.

. . .

> The **column-major lesson** again, on the card.

## Coalescing, measured {.smaller}

. . .

```julia
idx = CuArray(Int32.(((0:N-1) .* s) .% N .+ 1))   # stride s
a[idx]                                            # 20 M reads
```

. . .

| stride `s` | time | |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2.24 ms | coalesced |
| 33 | 5.40 ms | [**2.4× slower**]{style="background-color: yellow;"} |
| 1023 | 12.3 ms | 5.5× slower |

. . .

> ▶ Script: cell "6. Coalescing — locality again, at the scale of a warp"

. . .

> *"Only 2.4×?"* Which **other** bytes does `a[idx]` touch?

::: {.notes}
Same 20 M reads, different order: i ↦ (i·s mod N) + 1.
The stride must be COPRIME with N or it is not a permutation: gcd(32, 20_000_000)=32
would reread only 625k slots — a cache demo, not a coalescing demo. 33 works; 65
and 1025 do NOT (they share the factor 5). Script question: why must the index
be a permutation?
:::

## Testing that explanation 🔬 {.smaller}

. . .

`a[idx]` also reads `idx` and writes `out`, in order: only **1/3** of the bytes are punishable.

. . .

Index computed **in the kernel** → **1/2** punishable. The ratio **must rise**.

. . .

```julia
i = (blockIdx().x - 1) * blockDim().x + threadIdx().x   # my thread
j = ((i - 1) * s) % n + 1     # computed, never loaded
out[i] = a[j]
```

. . .

| stride 33 vs 1 | ratio |
|---|---|
| `a[idx]` (1/3) | 2.4× |
| kernel (1/2) | [**4.18×**]{style="background-color: yellow;"} |

. . .

> ▶ Script: cell "Test that explanation"

::: {.notes}
Kernel = a function run once per GPU thread; thread i handles element i.
The prediction held: an explanation you can test, and might have lost.
:::

# Monte-Carlo π {style="text-align: center;"}

## Monte-Carlo π on the card

. . .

```julia
function pi_gpu(n)
    x = CUDA.rand(Float32, n)            # in VRAM
    y = CUDA.rand(Float32, n)
    inside = (x.^2 .+ y.^2) .<= 1f0
    return 4 * sum(inside) / n           # one scalar back
end
```

- Same count as `count_in_disk`; 100 million GPU threads.
- Only **one number** crosses the bus.
- No shared counter: `sum` **reduces**.

. . .

> ▶ Script: cell "7. Monte-Carlo π on the GPU"

::: {.notes}
1f0 = 1 as a Float32. Minimize sharing, from 22 threads to 100 million.
:::

## π: which CPU do we compare to? {.smaller}

. . .

100 million points, `pi_gpu` ≈ **12 ms**:

. . .

| CPU baseline | GPU gain |
|---|---|
| `pi_cpu_vec` (allocates 2 × 400 MB) | ~35× |
| `count_in_disk`, scalar loop | [**~25×**]{style="background-color: yellow;"} |

- **Fair** baseline: the scalar loop. **~25×**.

. . .

> **Q3.** Threads module: 22 threads → 6.3×. Why is the card so far ahead?
>
> **Q4.** What in `pi_gpu` does **not** benefit from 100 M threads?

::: {.notes}
pi_cpu_vec mirrors pi_gpu but pays the allocation traffic; allocation-bound, very
load-sensitive. Threads deck: @spawn ×22 gave 6.3×. Q3: the card runs thousands of
threads and never leaves VRAM. Q4 answer: the final `sum` reduction (and the
launches) — the Amdahl part.
:::

## What we saw on the GPU

- `CuArray` in **VRAM**: same code, you pay the copy.
- **Bus** is expensive: bring back a scalar.
- Small jobs **lose**: batch.
- **Coalescing**: neighbor threads, neighbor addresses.

. . .
